_comment: Triage of the mutation runs over include/morph, produced by scripts/mutation.sh.
READ THIS FIRST: the survivor lists in `runs` below are NOT a worklist of missing
assertions, and roughly 42% of them are not findings at all. Both runs were taken with
Mull's `cxx_all` mutator set, which includes `cxx_remove_void_call` -- a mutator proven
broken for member/operator call sites in Mull 0.34.0 (see `mechanism_confirmed`: the
mutant's machine code disassembles byte-identical to its `_original`, so the call was
never removed and the suite was passed a program it had no reason to fail). Every one of
the 148 `cxx_remove_void_call` survivors in `runs[1]` -- 148 of 352 -- is a tool artifact
over code that was never mutated. Do not open an issue, write a test, or 'close a gap'
from one of those rows.
scripts/mutation.sh no longer enables that mutator (morph#434), so a future run will not
produce the artifact class again. No re-run has been made since: these numbers are the
last measured ones and are kept as the historical record, not as a current score. They
are not comparable to a post-change run -- a smaller mutant set changes the denominator,
and no score for the new set has been measured or estimated.
For the remaining mutator families, a survivor is still only weak evidence. `runs[1]`
records that four survivors sampled from three different headers were hand-applied to the
source and every one turned the suite red (`false_positive_finding`); those four were all
`cxx_remove_void_call`, which is now explained, but the sampling discipline stands:
re-confirm a survivor by hand before treating it as a gap.
The classes below still divide the list usefully -- `equivalent` entries are listed
individually with a reason each, because an unexplained exclusion is a suppression, and the
side channels are recorded separately so a future decision about logs is made about logs.
But the residual class is an upper bound on missing assertions, not a set of them.
TWO KINDS OF `line` LIVE IN THIS FILE, AND THEY MEAN OPPOSITE THINGS (morph#613).
Which one you are reading is decided by the section, so the split is written down here
rather than left to be inferred:
LIVE -- everything under `classes`. These describe a classification asserted to hold
NOW, so every citation in them points at CURRENT code and is carried as a structured
{file, line, source, reason} entry: `classes.equivalent.entries`, the two
`representative_sites` lists, and `classes.unasserted.shapes_worth_naming[1].sites`.
scripts/check_mutation_survivors.py resolves each of them by its `source` text on
every pull request and fails when the hint has drifted (morph#608, which found 5 of 7
already wrong and one off by 479 lines). When it fails, re-read the code at the line
it prints, confirm the reason still holds, and update `line`. Deleting an entry, or
editing its `source` to match some other line, is a triage nobody did. The gate finds
these by walking the whole document for {file, line, source} dicts, so a new live
citation is audited the moment it is written in that shape -- no script edit needed.
HISTORICAL -- `runs`, `false_positive_finding`, `mechanism_confirmed` and
`classification_2026_09_09`. These are records of dated campaigns, and their line
numbers point at the tree AS IT WAS WHEN THE CAMPAIGN RAN. They are not stale; they
are not about HEAD at all. Each such section carries a `revision` (plus a
`revision_provenance` saying how well it is established), so a citation resolves with
`git show <revision>:<path>` and keeps resolving forever. Resolving one against HEAD
is the reader error, and the gate deliberately does NOT audit them -- it prints how
many it left alone on every run, so a green tick never reads as 'all citations
checked'. Do not refresh a historical line number to match today's code: that would
falsify the record of what was measured.
Re-measure with: MULL_PREFIX=... bash scripts/mutation.sh core-forms

equivalent.meaning: No test could distinguish the mutant from the original, so the survivor is not a gap. Listed individually below.

entries.reason: The golden-ratio hash_combine mix. Every one of its three additions feeds a value used only as an unordered_map bucket index -- PairKeyHash is never serialised, never compared to a constant, and never pinned in docs/spec/pinned_facts.toml. Turning an addition into a subtraction yields a different hash, and an unordered container is required by the standard to behave correctly under any hash function, so no observable behaviour changes. What a test could assert -- that equal keys hash equally -- the mutant preserves, because it mutates the mixing arithmetic and not the inputs. Re-cited in morph#700 (morph#572 Part C): the mix moved from line 54 to line 79 and its text changed, because PairKeyHash became transparent and now hashes `std::string_view` rather than `std::string`. The mutant moved, it did not cease to exist -- the same three additions in the same mix are still there, on one line, still cxx_add_to_sub targets. Transparency adds one clause to the disposition rather than removing it: the `const std::pair<std::string, std::string>&` overload delegates to the `PairKeyView` body instead of hashing separately, so a mutation of these additions applies identically to the stored-key hash and the lookup hash. It cannot desynchronise the two and make a transparent `find()` miss a registered action -- the failure the functor's own doc comment names. Verified by reading the code at line 79 on this branch; the mutant count was not re-measured, the campaign being scheduled rather than per-PR.

Bridge::KeyHash is the same mix over the same kind of value, for _executors' bucket index, and equivalent for the same reason: the hash is internal to one unordered_map in one process and reaches no wire, no file and no assertion. Re-cited in morph#699: the mix moved from line 126 to line 144 and its text is unchanged, because KeyHash became transparent and the mix now lives in the KeyView overload rather than in the sole Key one. The mutant moved, it did not cease to exist -- the same three additions in the same mix are still there, on one line, still cxx_add_to_sub targets. Transparency adds one clause to the disposition rather than removing it: the `const Key&` overload delegates to the KeyView body instead of mixing separately, so a mutation of these additions applies identically to the stored-key hash and the lookup hash and cannot desynchronise the two into a transparent find() that misses a registered action. Verified by reading the code at line 144 on this branch; the mutant count was not re-measured, the campaign being scheduled rather than per-PR.

reserve() is a capacity hint. Its argument affects how many reallocations follow and nothing else -- the vector's contents, size and iteration order are identical whether it is told 42 or the real count. A test that could tell the difference would be asserting on an allocator, which is not part of this API.
A capacity hint on a std::string, equivalent for the same reason as the `aware.reserve(_changeAware.size());` entry in core/backend.hpp above.

A capacity hint on a std::vector, equivalent for the same reason as the `aware.reserve(_changeAware.size());` entry in core/backend.hpp above.
A capacity hint on a std::vector, equivalent for the same reason as the `aware.reserve(_changeAware.size());` entry in core/backend.hpp above.

side_channel_logging.meaning: Removing a log call survives because nothing in morph_tests captures log output.
side_channel_logging.reason: This is not equivalence -- a log line that stops being emitted is an observable change, and morph::log has a sink this suite could install. It is a deliberate absence of assertions on a diagnostic channel, and it is recorded separately from the gaps below so that a future decision to assert on logs (or not to) is made about logs rather than buried in a total.

representative_sites.reason: logError on an undecodable envelope -- the decode-failure arm of dispatchMessage. Deleting the call is invisible to morph_tests because no test installs a morph::log sink, so the survivor is a missing assertion on a diagnostic channel, not an equivalent mutant.
The one-line-per-request log every kind funnels through, on the successfully-decoded arm. Same disposition as the logError site above: observable in a deployment, unobserved by this suite.

side_channel_metrics.reason: include/morph/core/observability.hpp has a test file of its own (tests/test_observability.cpp), so unlike logging this is a surface the suite already asserts on -- just not on these eight call sites. Closer to a gap than logging is, and separated from it for that reason.

representative_sites.reason: The registerCount emission on LocalBackend::registerModel. Note for whoever refreshes this hint: the same statement appears character-for-character on the registerModelShared arm as well, so if this `line` ever drifts the gate will report the citation as ambiguous rather than printing a corrected line. That is the right outcome -- which of the two arms is meant is a question for a reader, not for a resolver -- and it is recorded here so the message is not a surprise. That happened in morph#700 (morph#572 Parts A and C), which reported lines [1149, 1168] and neither equal to the old hint 1087. Resolved by reading, not by guessing: at a9cb5649 line 1087 sat inside `registerModel(const std::string&, std::function<...>)`, and on this branch that same emission is line 1149, while 1168 is the `registerModelShared` twin. The disposition is unchanged -- neither arm's emission was touched by this branch.

The executeInFlight emission on the increment side of an execute. Its decrement twin inside the posted task is the same text after stripping, so the ambiguity note on the registerCount entry above applies here too -- and did, in morph#700, which reported lines [1318, 1371] against the old hint 1251. Resolved by reading: at a9cb5649 line 1251 was the emission immediately after `inFlightCounter->fetch_add(...)`, and on this branch that emission is line 1318, while 1371 is the post-`fetch_sub` twin inside the strand task. The disposition is unchanged -- this branch moved the surrounding `_strand.post` capture list, not the emission.

unasserted.meaning: Code morph_tests executes that the report says no test would notice being wrong. Four of these were sampled and hand-applied on 2026-09-03; all four turned the suite red. Treat an entry here as a site to check, not a gap that has been found.

consequences: morph#431's headline -- 'twenty places where the framework's response path can be
deleted and morph_tests stays green' -- is false as stated. The response path is
asserted; deleting it turns 34 cases red.
The 64.06% and 64.76% scores are lower bounds on the suite's real mutation score, and
the survivor list is an upper bound on the set of missing assertions. The caveat
recorded for the baseline run said the score 'can only be too high, never too low';
that was about test_outbox.cpp's scratch-file collisions and remains true of that
mechanism, but this one pushes the other way and is much larger.
cxx_remove_void_call is 148 of the 352 survivors, and remote.hpp and bridge.hpp -- both
header-only and included by many of morph_tests' 105 translation units -- are 211 of
them. Neither number should be read as a gap count until this is understood.
mechanism: Inferred from the shape of the result, not verified. Every affected site is in a header
compiled into many translation units, where each object carries its own copy of the
function and the linker keeps one. Mull embeds its mutants per object (the
`.mull_mutants` section) and the runner enables one by id; if the copy carrying the
enabled mutant is one the linker discarded, the running program is unmutated and the
mutant is scored as a survivor. That would make the effect specific to header-defined
code in a multi-TU binary, which matches where the survivors are concentrated -- but
it has not been confirmed against Mull's implementation.
what_would_change_the_verdict: A run in which a hand-applied survivor leaves the suite green would show that survivor
to be a real gap. Sampling four and finding four false positives does not prove all 352
are; it proves the report cannot be read site-by-site without this check.
Confirming the mechanism (or finding a Mull option that avoids it -- a single-TU
harness, or -fvisibility-inlines-hidden style deduplication control) would say how many

mechanism_confirmed.verdict: The linker-dedup hypothesis above is REFUTED. The real mechanism is a Mull codegen bug: cxx_remove_void_call's IR pass does not remove the call it claims to remove, for a member-function call site, in Mull 0.34.0.
mechanism_confirmed.verification_status: measured, 2026-09-04, in an isolated WSL Ubuntu 24.04 environment, Mull-19 0.34.0 / LLVM 19.1.7, clang 19.1.7 -- a different build (Windows) and toolchain from every prior measurement in this file, so the finding is not specific to one environment's linker. Mull 0.34.0 (checked 2026-09-04) is the project's latest release, so there is no newer version to retest the mechanism against.
mechanism_confirmed.revision_provenance: PARTIAL, and stated as such. 567168b2 is the commit that wrote this section; `git cat-file -t` confirms it. It does NOT pin the measurement, because the measurement was not made against this repository: the four programs under `method` below are standalone .cpp/.hpp files reproduced inline there, built outside the tree. This section carries no line citations into include/morph, so there is nothing here for a revision to resolve. The field is recorded anyway so every dated section in this file states a revision and a reader does not have to work out which ones a revision would help.
method: The linker-dedup hypothesis predicts the bug disappears once a function has only one copy
to be discarded -- i.e. a single translation unit, linked alone, with no duplicate object
to compete with. Four minimal C++ programs were built, each ONE .cpp including a header
with an inline function containing exactly one call site, compiled with
-fpass-plugin=mull-ir-frontend-19 and linked ALONE (no second TU, no dedup possible by
construction). Each was run under mull-runner-19 and, separately, its mutant machine code
was read directly with objdump to check whether the claimed removal actually happened.

results.case: holder.attachIdentity(std::string{primary}) -- a member call with a temporary argument, one statement, last in its function
results.single_tu_result: Survived, even with zero possibility of linker dedup
results.disassembly_finding: The mutant function body (labelled cxx_remove_void_call:...) is byte-identical to the mull__..._original twin: both still `call Holder::attachIdentity`. The removal was never emitted.

results.case: holder.attachIdentity(primary) -- same member call, no temporary, argument passed as a plain named value
results.single_tu_result: Survived, same disassembly signature (call still present in both copies)
results.note: Rules out 'destructor cleanup on a temporary blocks the removal' as the cause -- there is no temporary here and the bug is identical.

results.case: bumpCounter() -- a free function call, void return, discarded, same statement shape
results.disassembly_finding: The mutant function body genuinely omits the call; only the destructor/cleanup code remains. This confirms the IR pass and the runner's activation plumbing (the getenv-gated dispatch) both work correctly in general -- the defect is scoped to the member-call shape, not the mutator or the runner as a whole.

Every one of this section's line citations was re-resolved at it with `git show` and each names the code it claims -- the Feistel round function, the three hash-combine sites, the fingerprint accumulation, the three permute() lines, and the four `survivor_list_unreliable` samples.
_comment: Classification of run[2]'s 199 survivors (morph#453 item A).
Updated 2026-09-10. The headline finding is NOT a classification: sampling
showed the survivor list itself is unreliable -- 5 of 6 sampled survivors
are killed by the existing suite when the same mutation is applied by hand.
See survivor_list_unreliable below and morph#510. Classifying the remaining
entries against this list would be measuring the tool, not the test suite.
classification_2026_09_09.method: Clustered by (mutator, source shape), then assessed cluster by cluster against what the code actually promises -- not by writing an assertion per mutant, which the issue's own constraint rules out.

sites: core/remote.hpp:157,158,160,162 -- OpaqueIdGenerator::mix, the Feistel round function
reason: The Feistel construction (L,R) -> (R, L ^ F(R)) is invertible for ANY round function F, which permute()'s own doc comment states ('this regardless of the round function'). Mutating inside mix() therefore preserves the only property the code claims -- that distinct counters yield distinct ids -- so no honest test can kill these.

The hash-combine sites are the same shape: nothing in the contract fixes a hash VALUE, only determinism and adequate distribution. A test that killed these would assert a specific hash constant, pinning an implementation detail -- exactly the 'test with no reason to exist' the issue warns against.

real_gap_closed.finding: The existing bijection test drives counters 1..20000, all of which have a ZERO high half. It therefore passes whether or not permute() uses the top 32 bits at all -- it cannot distinguish a 64-bit permutation from one that ignores half its input.
real_gap_closed.measured: Simulated against the real round function over 20000 counters that do exercise the high half: '>>' -> '<<' collapses 20000 ids to 1; the Feistel '^' -> '|' collapses them to 1256. Both are catastrophic collisions in opaque model ids, and both are invisible to the existing sample.
real_gap_closed.closed_by: tests/test_opaque_model_ids.cpp, 'OpaqueIdGenerator is a bijection over counters that exercise the high half'. Kills the :142 and :145 mutants. The :148 mutant still survives -- 'hi >> 32' yields 0 so the id degenerates to its low half, which stays distinct for these inputs; killing it needs a probe on the id's high bits, not a distinctness count.

unclassified.note: 16 classified (13 equivalent, 3 real and closed). The rest are NOT classified, and per survivor_list_unreliable above, classifying them against this run is the wrong next step.
unclassified.next_step: Fix or characterise the tooling first (morph#510). A survivor list where 5 of 6 samples are false is not a worklist.

survivor_list_unreliable.status: Reproduced behaviourally, one of them on a worktree at the campaign's own revision (adfe8e5f) with its own build. Mechanism NOT established -- Mull is not installed here, so no disassembly, unlike morph#434.

samples.result: suite hangs; mull-runner's --timeout 60000 counts a timeout as detected

samples.verdict: genuinely equivalent -- the initialiser is dead, overwritten by `started = backend->attachModelAsync(...)` on the next statement
samples.note: Recorded 2026-09-09 and kept verbatim. morph#571 removed that verb and the `bool started` initialiser with it, so neither the line nor the statement exists in the tree any more. This is a record of what a sampling run measured on that revision, not a description of today's code; rewriting it to match would destroy the measurement.

important: The defect is per-mutant, not per-family: cxx_init_const produced one genuine equivalent AND one mis-report. An earlier draft of this entry blamed whole families and was wrong.
So the 199 cannot be bulk-reclassified by mutator. What the sampling establishes is that the list is not trustworthy enough to classify against by hand.
ruled_out: Test-scope mismatch: scripts/mutation.sh's core-forms scope runs tests/morph_tests, the same binary and full suite, with no filter passed to mull-runner.
Revision mismatch: the 140-failure measurement is on adfe8e5f itself and the quoted source line matches character-for-character.
Wholesale mutant-selection failure: 574 of 773 were killed in the same run, so the mechanism works in general.
survivor_list_unreliable.consequence: The 199-survivor baseline overstates real gaps by an unknown but large margin. It still works as a relative ratchet for morph#408's gate, since the artifacts are stable run to run.
